A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and retain the core framework and experiments. Their main texts, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison across reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original trained-network experiments on synthetic Ising and linear teacher–student tasks, comparing empirical predictions and output covariances with theoretical results in Figures 1–6.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original MNIST evaluations, nonlinear network experiments, and tests of directional learning under varying input structure.

M1.justification: v1 develops the linear-network procedure and leaves nonlinear extensions to future work. v2 incorporates nonlinear activations and develops both cumulant-based and variational Gaussian approximation procedures for their prediction kernels and self-consistency equations (Appendices A.1.2 and A.2.3). The original linear framework remains.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond the original Ising and linear teacher–student tasks to binary MNIST classification and nonlinear teacher–student regression with linear and cubic Hermite target components. Figure 11 also introduces structured and unstructured Ising input scenarios with varying signal strength.

E2.justification: Matched original experiments retain NNGP, Li–Sompolinsky rescaling, and the same approximation variants. New experiments reuse NNGP and scalar rescaling, using activation kernels for nonlinear networks. The change from 'One-Loop Rescaling' to 'One-Loop simpl.' does not introduce a different comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds an erf-network sample-size sweep using component learnability, with N = 1,000, D = 30, and 4,000 test points, plus MNIST evaluation settings. Section 6 also removes trace normalization from the directional measure Phi, although this cancels in the plotted directional ratios. Original linear-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Figure 11 compares structured and unstructured kernels and varies the Ising signal parameter to test coherent amplification of input structure. Figure 5 separately analyzes learning of linear and cubic target components as sample size increases, probing where adaptive and rescaling predictions diverge.

E5.justification: Both versions report different initialization seeds, averaging 100 networks for Ising predictions and 5,000 for teacher–student output covariances. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or stated repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Figure 5 reports increasing cubic-component learnability captured by the adaptive approximation while NNGP and rescaling remain near zero. Figures 6–9 add MNIST and nonlinear Ising results, and Figure 11 adds input-structure-dependent amplification findings. These are new results under added conditions; v1 Figures 5–6 are retained as v2 Figures 10 and 12.

T1.justification: v2 adds nonlinear-prior cumulant derivations, variational Gaussian self-consistency equations, an analytical argument for coherent kernel amplification, and Appendix B's derivation connecting another readout-weight scaling regime. It also revises the mathematical definition of Phi and introduces component learnability. The original linear derivations largely remain.

C1.justification: v1's demonstrated directional-learning contribution concerns output covariance in linear networks. v2 explicitly extends its contribution to nonlinear networks and claims differences in mean predictions and sample-complexity class, supported by the new nonlinear experiment. This substantially broadens the abstract, introduction, and discussion beyond the retained linear rescaling connection.

C2.justification: v2 explains cooperative amplification of coherent input and target structure and connects nonlinear directional learning to sample efficiency. It distinguishes rescaling equivalence under the cumulant approximation from its breakdown under finer approximations. The earlier linear-only limitation and nonlinear future-work statement are replaced by discussion of the remaining shallow-network scope.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access DOI and Appendix C.2/Algorithm 1 documenting solver initialization, annealing across scaling regimes, and stated O(P^3) computational cost. The existing Langevin training description and 10,000-step equilibration statement remain; the new solver documentation does not establish a change to the original experiments.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands positioning through maximal-update scaling, representation-learning frameworks, and additional deep-linear results. New Appendix B explicitly derives the relationship to van Meegen and Sompolinsky's alternative scaling and distinguishes weight concentration from output concentration. This extends the theoretical positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, related-work passages, and discussion receive targeted rewriting. General statements are separated from the exact linear case, and the appendices gain more specific subsections. Much of the original prose and the main seven-section narrative remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial graphical presentations of nonlinear component learning, MNIST evaluations, nonlinear Ising predictions, and kernel-structure controls, plus an algorithm panel. Existing figures are retained with relocation, caption, schematic, and legend edits; the original appendix figures are renumbered rather than removed.

improvement.justification: The nonlinear treatment and component-learning experiment address v1's explicit linear-only limitation, while MNIST and kernel-structure controls materially strengthen validation. Solver guidance and a code-access DOI also improve reproducibility information. Some added mathematics remains internally inconsistent, notably Eq. (72) omitting the inverse present in Eq. (26), but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in explanatory scope and empirical support.
